newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Wives of HK Chinese tycoons pick silk for handover.
newsitem.headline: Wives of HK Chinese tycoons pick silk for handover.

text.p: Discard the Dior. Leave behind the Yves St Laurent. A silk, figure-hugging cheongsam definitely is the designer dress for the handover party.
So says that arbiter of fashion and taste, The Hong Kong Tatler magazine.
Jill Triptree, editor of the socialites' glossy bible, forecasts that the distinctive dress with the slit up the thigh will be all the rage for the wives of Chinese multimillionaires.
For Hong Kong's beautiful people plan to celebrate in style on June 30 when Britain hands the teeming metropolis back to China after 156 years of colonial rule.
"A lot of people will go for a Chinese look with their own tailor doing up a cheongsam for them," Triptree told Reuters.
The magazine is a mirror of social change in the declining years of British rule.
Gone are the days when matrons of expatriate High Society reigned supreme at candle-lit dinners on The Peak, the mist-covered mountain where they lived in isolated splendour.
Now the big charity balls are run by the Tai-Tai's (Mandarin for Madam or Wife) whose worthy causes range from surgeries to orphanages in mainland China.
The Tatler produces a list every year of the top 500 on Hong Kong's hyperactive social scene. Expatriates now make up just 20 percent of the total.
Hong Kong may be heading into uncharted political and economic waters from July 1 but Triptree said: "The social scene has already been handed over."
In a sign of the times, the magazine appointed Chinese Malaysian Ong Chin Huat as social editor.
He says of the indefatigable tai-tai's "They lead the most incredible lives. They eat the best food, the most exotic foods like bird's nest soup, shark's fin soup, abalone."

"They buy the most expensive clothes -- Versace, Chanel. They fly to Paris three to four times a year just for shopping. They buy the most expensive jewels. They drive the most expensive cars, they really pamper themselves," he told Sky Television.
As China modernises at breakneck pace and living standards keep on climbing, the magazine feels the time is right for a mainland move.
"We are going into China with Tatler," Triptree said. "We feel it will go down well. Shanghai is where we would like to start."

Taipans (foreign dynastic tycoons) once dominated Hong Kong, with the merchant princes from the great British trading houses ruling over business while their wives were the social empresses of the colony.
Now Tiptree says of the old expatriate aristocracy in the leadup to the handover: "The feeling among them is, It is time to step aside. Sit back and let the Chinese have their time."
